newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin recovering from serious illness - doctor.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin recovering from serious illness - doctor.

text.p: Doctors said on Wednesday that President Boris Yeltsin was recovering after a week in hospital with pneumonia, but warned that the illness was serious and complications were always possible.
Chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov said Yeltsin should stay in hospital this week. "Beyond that it will depend on the course of his illness," he said.

Yeltsin, 65, was taken to hospital last Wednesday with pneumonia, which Mironov said had developed out of a heavy cold caught after Yeltsin had been to the banya, the Russian-style steam bath which the president particularly relishes.

Doctors have denied any link to the recurrent heart problems Yeltsin suffered in 1995 and 1996. On Friday, Mironov said heart bypass surgery like that which Yeltsin underwent last November sometimes resulted in complications like pneumonia, but that he hoped the operation had protected rather than weakened him.

Mironov, who said last Friday Yeltsin would stay in hospital just another three days, explained the apparent extension by saying said the president at first insisted on leaving hospital after that time but had since been persuaded to stay longer.

Yeltsin underwent a quintuple heart bypass operation on November 5 after a reported third heart attack just before the July 3 second round of the presidential election. He has spent only a few days in the Kremlin since the poll.
Mironov said Yeltsin had become more active in the last few days, although doctors were trying to limit him. But the double pneumonia, affecting both lungs, was not to be taken lightly.
"I should say that this is a fairly serious illness, which of course brings with it a whole range of possible complications," he added. "In this respect, there will be a daily doctors' meeting."
Doctors still assumed the president would be fit to attend a summit of leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States, due to take place in Moscow towards the end of January.
Mironov said Yeltsin probably caught cold after the banya and that this had developed into bronchitis and then pneumonia.

Opposition deputies in the communist-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament have begun discussing if Yeltsin's prolonged illness would give them grounds to remove him from office, although they admit there is little chance of success.
Mironov, referring to Russian labour law which counts a period of sickness from the date when an invalid last worked said Yeltsin had officially only been off work for a week.

He said at first he had been confined to bed but that now he was working on documents. "Sometimes he gets up at 3.30, 4 o'clock and works on documents and then three hours later he might sleep for another hour and a half," Mironov said.
"Of course we try to limit his workload because the illness he now has is quite treacherous," he said.
Mironov said that one of the main complications a patient like Yeltsin could develop was oedema -- waterlogging of the lungs caused by heart problems.
"Fortunately we have avoided that. It was one of the reasons he was taken to hospital, because it is a very dangerous situation, especially with double pneumonia."
"The second case is some deterioration of the capacity of the heart muscle, that is cardiac deficiency. This, fortunately is also under control and there have been no noticeable turns for the worse."

"But of course the illness leaves its mark on all organs and systems and lung disease, of course, is close and linked to cardiac problems," said adding that Renat Akchurin, who gave Yeltsin his bypass, is a permanent member of the medical team.
